bib.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed only; plot-axis number lines not analysed.

question: Can language models evaluate the validity of their own answers (P(True)) and be trained to predict whether they know the answer to a question (P(IK))?
hypothesis: Models that are calibrated on multiple choice and True/False questions can be used to self-evaluate their own samples, and a trained P(IK) head can capture what the model knows and generalise across tasks.
contributions: Large models are well calibrated on lettered multiple choice and on True/False; 'none of the above' hurts accuracy and calibration; RLHF miscalibration largely fixed by a single temperature.
Self-evaluation (P(True)) of model samples without finetuning, improved by showing five of the model's own T=1 samples.
P(IK) value-head finetuning: partial generalisation across tasks, poor OOD calibration, responds to source material and hints.
Comparison of two models with different pretraining data.

method.summary: Pretrained Anthropic LMs (800M to 52B) are evaluated for calibration on multiple choice (BIG Bench, MMLU, TruthfulQA, LogiQA, QuALITY) and True/False formats, prompted (not trained) to give P(True) for their own T=1 samples on five generative tasks, and finetuned with a value head to give P(IK). Calibration is measured with ECE, Brier, AUROC.
method.task: calibration, self-evaluation of sampled answers, and prediction of whether a model can answer a question

datasets.name: BIG Bench multiple choice (all), MMLU, TruthfulQA, LogiQA, QuALITY
datasets.split: few-shot examples drawn at random from the test evaluation itself; BIG Bench within subtask, MMLU across whole eval
datasets.preprocessing: Lettered options, answer by label; or one correct plus one random incorrect answer as True/False (twice as many problems); or last option replaced with 'none of the above'

datasets.name: TriviaQA
datasets.split: train for P(IK) finetuning; held-out test questions for evaluation
datasets.preprocessing: 10-shot prompt of random TriviaQA items; 30 answers sampled at T=1; correctness by string comparison

datasets.name: Python function synthesis (GitHub-scraped)
datasets.source: scraped Python repos with a 'test' file; functions with at least half the lines covered by passing tests
datasets.preprocessing: 0-shot; partial file with function def and docstring at the end

datasets.name: GSM8k
datasets.preprocessing: 10-shot with reasoning; scored by number after ####; only 52B evaluated; ground truth P(IK) binarised at 0.25 in histograms (0.5 in Table 1)

models.name: Anthropic pretrained LMs
models.architecture: inferred: decoder-only transformer, as Bai et al. 2022 (paper says identical architecture and training setup to that work)

other.code_share: about 10% of pretraining distribution; not finetuned on Python

models.name: HH RLHF policies
models.architecture: finetuned from the base LMs as in Bai et al. 2022

other.pretraining: A: four repetitions of a high quality dataset; B: one copy of it mixed with one copy of a larger lower-quality web distribution

training.objective: cross-entropy on P(IK) value-head logit; 30 T=1 samples per question each give a hard IK/IDK label (e.g. 20 correct and 10 incorrect gives 20 IK copies and 10 IDK copies); loss backpropagated only at last input token
training.lr: 1/3 of the original pretraining learning rate

other.scope: entire model finetuned along with value head
other.note: P(True) is prompted only, no training; pretraining of base LMs not described here

inference.decoding: T=1 sampling for answers evaluated; T=0 sample used in Appendix B
inference.samples: 30 T=1 samples per question for P(IK) ground truth; 5 T=1 samples total shown in the comparison P(True) format; N=200 samples for entropy; 30 stuffed samples for mean token loss
inference.prompting: Letter-labelled options; True/False format '(A) True (B) False'; P(True) prompt with six examples (Appendix A.5) or 20-shot; few-shot examples drawn from the test set itself

parameters.ground-truth P(IK): fraction of T=1 samples correct, binarised at 0.5 (0.25 for some GSM8k plots)

metrics.name: ECE
metrics.definition: mean absolute difference between prediction and frequency over 10 equal-count bins, top predictions only

metrics.name: RMS calibration error
metrics.definition: root mean square of the same

metrics.name: AUROC
metrics.definition: discriminating known from unknown questions, or correct from incorrect samples; chance 0.5

metrics.name: Brier score
metrics.definition: mean (p-c)^2, p = P(True), c = correctness; chance 0.25 on binary tasks

baselines: one-example prompt vs comparison-example prompt vs 20-shot
loss of T=0 sample, entropy of answer distribution, stuffed-sample loss (Appendix B)
eval.protocol: Single reported runs; no seeds, error bars or significance tests stated. Most results appear only as plots.

limits: Only pretrained models; the authors say RLHF models will not be so well calibrated and methods may not work as well.
Pretraining is human imitation; the analysis does not separate truth from what humans say.
Only five sampling-based datasets; capability-trend and generalisation observations limited in power and scope.
Almost all calibration and P(True) results are plots; no seeds, error bars or significance tests.
Small models look well calibrated on hard tasks only by predicting P(True) near 0.
P(IK) may track question difficulty rather than self-knowledge; the 12B A/B test shows only about a 6% difference.
Few-shot examples for P(True) are drawn from the test set itself.
Natural-language P(IK) approach abandoned after early experiments.
Models cannot tell their own tokens from tokens given by a third party (footnote 4).

terms.definition: The probability a model assigns to the proposition that a speciﬁc sample is the correct answer to a question.
The probability a model assigns to "I know", i.e. the proposition that it will answer a given question correctly when samples are generated at unit temperature.
The fraction of unit temperature samples to a question that are correct.
